patient.name: Marcus Delgado
patient.chiefComplaint: Explosion victim with bleeding leg wound, burns, and hearing loss

history.hpi: Patient was working near a propane tank that exploded, throwing him several feet. He has an actively bleeding shrapnel wound to the right thigh, partial-thickness burns to his face and forearms, and reports ringing in his ears with difficulty hearing questions. He is anxious and repeatedly asks crew to speak up.
history.lastOralIntake: Lunch approximately 3 hours prior to the explosion
history.events: Propane tank explosion at a work site; patient thrown backward, struck by shrapnel and debris; coworkers called 911 immediately

scene.dispatch: Explosion reported, multiple possible patients, industrial work site
scene.location: Outdoor equipment yard at a commercial work site, patient found approximately 20 feet from the blast seat, debris scattered around
scene.safety: Scene secured by fire/hazmat for secondary explosion risk before EMS access; structural debris and scattered sharp fragments nearby
scene.bystanders: Two coworkers present, one applied direct pressure to the leg wound with a t-shirt before EMS arrival
visualCues: Actively bleeding shrapnel wound to right anterior thigh
Partial-thickness burns to face and both forearms with singed hair
Debris and shrapnel scattered across the scene
Patient repeatedly says "what?" and leans in to hear questions
Torn, blood-soaked clothing on the right leg

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 33-year-old male with an actively bleeding right thigh wound from shrapnel, partial-thickness burns to the face and forearms, and apparent hearing loss/tinnitus from the blast overpressure. He is alert but anxious and has difficulty hearing questions.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking clearly but has difficulty hearing questions
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, mildly diminished breath sounds on the right
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Active bleeding from right thigh wound, radial pulses present but rapid
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities; guarding right leg due to pain
otherFindings: Actively bleeding shrapnel wound, right anterior thigh, coworker applying direct pressure
Partial-thickness burns to face and both forearms, approximately 15% BSA
Tinnitus and apparent hearing loss, possible tympanic membrane rupture
Anxious, repeatedly asks crew to repeat themselves
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "What? I can't hear you well — my leg, it won't stop bleeding!"

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform MARCH primary survey prioritizing hemorrhage control over burns/hearing loss
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Optimal trauma care requires a structured approach to the patient emphasizing first control of massive hemorrhage using MARCH (Massive hemorrhage, Airway, Respiratory/Breathing, Circulation, Head injury/Hypothermia)
expectedActions.rationale: The visible burns and hearing complaint are distracting but not immediately life-threatening; uncontrolled hemorrhage is.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply commercial tourniquet 2-3 in proximal to right thigh wound; mark placement time
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Tourniquet should be placed 2–3 inches proximal to wound, not over a joint, and tightened until bleeding stops and distal pulse is eliminated Mark the time of tourniquet placement prominently on the patient and in the patient care report
expectedActions.rationale: Survival is markedly improved when a tourniquet is placed before shock develops.

expectedActions.shortAction: Continually reassess for blast lung injury and possible airway burn
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Continually reassess for blast lung injury. Consider possible thermal or chemical burns to the airway
expectedActions.rationale: Blast overpressure injury can cause delayed-onset pulmonary barotrauma that isn't apparent on first contact.

transitions.condition: Crew performs a MARCH primary survey, prioritizing hemorrhage control before addressing the burns or hearing loss, and applies a tourniquet to the actively bleeding right thigh wound.
Crew is distracted by the visible burns and the patient's hearing loss/confusion, delaying tourniquet application on the actively bleeding thigh wound while blood loss continues.

phases.name: Massive hemorrhage controlled first
phases.description: Crew immediately applies a tourniquet to the actively bleeding right thigh wound before addressing the burns or hearing complaint, following the MARCH massive-hemorrhage-first priority, then continues the primary survey.
phases.triggerCondition: After the initial hemorrhage assessment, the crew immediately applies a tourniquet to the actively bleeding right thigh wound before addressing the burns or hearing loss, per the MARCH massive-hemorrhage-first priority, and continues the primary survey with attention to blast-specific injury patterns.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, breath sounds not yet fully reassessed
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Bleeding controlled, tourniquet in place, distal pulse absent below tourniquet as expected
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities aside from guarded right leg
otherFindings: Commercial tourniquet applied 2-3 inches proximal to thigh wound, time marked
Burns and hearing complaint not yet addressed
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That hurts, but at least it's not gushing anymore."

expectedActions.shortAction: Needle decompression right 2nd ICS midclavicular line for tension pneumothorax
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If the patient has evidence of tension pneumothorax, perform needle decompression consider tension pneumothorax and perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation; may need second or third needle decompression on same side if there is a rush of air but patient again has symptoms
expectedActions.rationale: Untreated tension pneumothorax rapidly progresses to obstructive shock and cardiac arrest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access; administer NS per Burns Guideline given TBSA and shock signs
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access with two large bore IVs or IOs If the patient is burned, administer normal saline (NS) or lactated Ringer's (LR) per the Burns Guideline
expectedActions.rationale: IV access supports both fluid resuscitation for the burns and readiness for shock management.

expectedActions.shortAction: Rapid total-body exposure exam including log roll; keep patient warm
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Rapid evaluation of entire skin surface, including back (log roll), to identify blunt or penetrating injuries Keep patient warm to prevent hypothermia
expectedActions.rationale: Blast injuries can hide additional penetrating wounds that aren't obvious on initial survey.

transitions.condition: Crew proceeds to reassess breath sounds bilaterally, noting decreased sounds on the right consistent with barotrauma, and prepares for needle decompression if tension physiology develops.
Crew continues focusing on burn dressing and IV access while the patient's respiratory distress, hypotension, and tracheal deviation worsen without needle decompression.

phases.name: Breath sounds reassessed on right
phases.description: With hemorrhage controlled, the crew reassesses breathing and finds progressively diminished breath sounds on the right with rising respiratory distress, tachycardia, and borderline hypotension — early tension physiology from blast barotrauma — and performs needle decompression while managing the burns and IV fluids.
phases.triggerCondition: After hemorrhage is controlled, the crew reassesses breathing and finds progressively diminished breath sounds on the right with rising respiratory distress and borderline hypotension, consistent with developing tension pneumothorax from blast barotrauma.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Markedly diminished breath sounds on the right, mild tracheal deviation, increasing work of breathing
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Bleeding controlled, radial pulses present but rapid and thready, mild jugular distension
otherFindings: Partial-thickness burns to face and forearms not yet dressed

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to trauma center with burn capability per field triage guideline; minimize scene time
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Primary transport to a trauma or burn center is preferable, whenever possible Decisions regarding transport destination should be based on the ACS-COT 2022 National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients
expectedActions.rationale: Multi-system blast injury with burns requires a facility capable of managing both trauma and burn care.

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vitals, breath sounds, and tourniquet serially en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor patient for deterioration over time with serial vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and repeat neurologic status assessment Tourniquet should be reassessed at every stage of patient movement to ensure ongoing hemorrhage control.
expectedActions.rationale: Blast patients can deteriorate from occult injuries not apparent on the initial survey.

transitions.if: Decompression relieves pressure, packaged for transport
transitions.condition: Needle decompression produces an audible rush of air; breath sounds and vitals improve. The patient is packaged with the tourniquet visible, burns dressed, and fluids running for transport to a trauma/burn center.

phases.name: Decompression relieves pressure, packaged for transport
phases.description: Needle decompression relieves the tension physiology; breath sounds and vitals improve. The crew completes burn dressing, secures IV fluids, and packages the patient with a clearly marked tourniquet for transport to a trauma center with burn capability.
phases.triggerCondition: After needle decompression relieves the tension physiology, the crew completes burn dressing, secures IV fluids, and packages the patient with a clearly marked tourniquet for transport, targeting a trauma center with burn capability.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved, breath sounds now symmetric bilaterally
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Stable, tourniquet marked and visible, IV fluids infusing
otherFindings: Burns dressed with dry sterile dressings
Tourniquet time clearly marked and visible, not covered
Hearing loss persists but patient is calmer

phases.name: Tourniquet delayed for burns/hearing
phases.description: The crew is drawn to the dramatic-looking burns and the patient's hearing loss/confusion, delaying tourniquet application on the actively bleeding thigh wound. Ongoing blood loss drives the patient into hemorrhagic shock.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew is distracted by the visible burns and the patient's hearing loss/confusion, delaying tourniquet application on the actively bleeding right thigh wound; ongoing blood loss drives the patient into hemorrhagic shock.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Active bleeding continues from right thigh, weak thready pulses

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize hemorrhagic shock; apply tourniquet immediately, consider TXA
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: First stop severe external and extremity hemorrhage with extremity tourniquets or appropriate wound packing with hemostatic gauze. Consider tranexamic acid (TXA) for injury associated with hemorrhagic shock if within three hours of injury
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed hemorrhage control is the most preventable cause of trauma death; immediate correction is still critical once recognized.

phases.name: Decompression delayed despite worsening signs
phases.description: The crew continues focusing on burn dressing and IV access while the patient's respiratory distress, hypotension, and tracheal deviation worsen without needle decompression — a progressing, untreated tension pneumothorax.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew continues focusing on burn dressing and IV access while the patient's respiratory distress, hypotension, and tracheal deviation worsen without needle decompression, consistent with a progressing untreated tension pneumothorax.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Absent breath sounds on the right, severe accessory muscle use
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Weak, thready pulses, marked jugular venous distension
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Unable to speak in full sentences, gasping

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize tension pneumothorax; needle decompress right 2nd ICS immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If absent or diminished breath sounds in a hypotensive trauma patient, especially those with chest trauma and/or tracheal deviation, consider tension pneumothorax and perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation
expectedActions.rationale: Untreated tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock and cardiac arrest if not decompressed promptly.
